body.heading: Three quantities, one watery picture
paragraphs: Electricity becomes much easier to picture if you think of water flowing through pipes. Voltage is the pressure in the system — how hard the water is being pushed, supplied by a pump or a raised tank. In a circuit, the battery or power supply provides this electrical pressure, measured in volts.

Current is the flow itself: how much water passes a point each second. Electrically, it is how much charge flows per second, measured in amperes (amps). Resistance is anything that narrows or roughens the pipe — a partial blockage that resists the flow, measured in ohms.

body.heading: How the three lean on each other
paragraphs: The three quantities obey a tidy rule, Ohm's law: current equals voltage divided by resistance. Raise the pressure and more water flows; tighten the blockage and less flows, even at the same pressure. Double the voltage across a component and (for most simple components) the current through it doubles.

Every electrical device is a designed resistance. A heater is a resistance chosen to draw a large current and turn the energy into heat; an LED is a frugal resistance that sips current and turns a share of it into light. Fuses and cables are chosen so the expected currents never overheat them.

body.heading: Where the water picture ends
paragraphs: The water analogy is a ladder worth climbing and then leaving behind. Real electrons do not slosh, spill or speed up downhill, and voltage is not quite pressure — but for predicting how a torch, a kettle or a house circuit behaves, the picture rarely misleads beginners.

It also explains everyday ratings at a glance. A phone charger marked 5 volts and 2 amps can push charge at a certain rate; a 230-volt mains socket offers far more pressure, which is why it can run a kettle — and why it demands far more respect.

description: Voltage is pressure, current is flow, resistance is the blockage — a water-pipe picture that makes Ohm's law almost visible.
